text: Scant means very little — barely enough, far less than you'd want or expect. When the article says there is scant evidence that grocers earn excessive profits, it means the proof is almost nonexistent: hardly anything to point to at all.

Literally, to gouge is to dig or scoop a chunk out of something. Applied to prices, it means overcharging people unfairly by exploiting power over them — “price gouging” — scooping extra money out of shoppers who have nowhere else to go. The article's point: without market concentration, grocers simply don't have the power to gouge anyone.

Opportunism is grabbing whatever chance benefits you, even when it's a little unfair — an opportunist sees an opening and pounces, principles aside. Grocers stand accused of it: using the confusion of inflation as cover to raise prices further than their costs required. The article checks the numbers and finds that evidence “hard to find.”

A populist politician wins support by championing “ordinary people” against a villainous “elite” — often with simple, satisfying stories about exactly who is to blame. The subtitle calls the blame-the-supermarkets story populist because it names a convenient villain instead of wrestling with the messier truth.

Slop is the sloppy, semi-liquid mush fed to pigs — and lately the go-to insult for lazy, low-quality content. Calling the greedy-shops theory “populist slop” dismisses it as junk food for the mind: easy to swallow, zero nourishment.

The hero of Victor Hugo's novel “Les Misérables” (and the musical): imprisoned for nineteen years for stealing a single loaf of bread to feed his sister's starving children — literature's most famous grocery bill.

The “demon barber of Fleet Street” from the famous horror musical: he murders his customers, and his partner Mrs Lovett bakes them into her meat pies — that's what the article means by her “source of free meat.” Gruesome, but her pie-shop economics were unbeatable.

An unholy alliance is a partnership between parties who have no business teaming up — one that feels wrong or sinister. Mrs Lovett joining forces with a murderous barber for pie filling is about as unholy as an alliance gets.

Volatile means liable to change suddenly and sharply — a volatile chemical can explode; a volatile temper can blow up; volatile prices swing wildly without warning. Housing and fuel are “recently volatile expenses”: their prices have been jumping around.

In economics, “nominal” means measured in plain dollar numbers, without adjusting for inflation. Grocery prices beating “nominal wage growth” means food prices rose faster than paychecks did — so even people earning more dollars can afford less food than before.

To be afflicted by something is to suffer under it, the way you'd suffer a disease — an affliction is a painful burden. Casting rising grocery bills as something countries are “afflicted by” sets up the article's question: who, or what, caused the outbreak?

Discontent is simmering unhappiness — a population that is not content with how things are going. Grocery-price discontent is what's “inviting all kinds of intervention”: unhappy voters attract politicians with fixes to sell.

An intervention is stepping into a situation to change how it would naturally play out. Here it's governments stepping into the grocery business — opening their own stores, pressuring prices down, banning charges they call “excessive” — rather than leaving the market alone.

To cruise to victory is to win easily — gliding to the finish line without much of a fight. Zohran Mamdani cruised to victory in New York partly by promising to tackle the cost of living, which shows how politically powerful grocery anger has become.

The mainstream is where the majority swims — an idea “goes mainstream” when it jumps from the fringe into normal, everyday acceptance. State-run grocery stores were once a fringe notion in Canada; then a champion of the concept was elected to lead a major party.
Not a trophy-winner here: a champion of an idea is its devoted public fighter — someone who campaigns for it (think “championing a cause”). Avi Lewis is a champion of the state-grocery-store concept.

To meddle is to interfere in something that isn't really yours to control — the word always carries disapproval. Governments trying “to meddle with prices directly” are reaching in and pushing prices around by hand, which economists generally wince at.

Suasion is a rare, fancy word for persuasion — moving someone with pressure and words rather than commands. “By suasion or by force” covers both routes in the article: Trump talking Walmart into cutting prices, versus Australia passing a law that outright bans “excessive” ones.

Nothing to do with the office supply: staple products are the everyday basics households buy constantly — bread, milk, rice, ground beef. A “staple” food is one a diet is built on, which is why cutting prices on staples makes headlines.
At someone's behest means at their command or urgent request — a formal, slightly royal-sounding word. Trump claimed Walmart lowered its prices at his behest: because he told it to.

To deem is to officially judge something to be so — a verdict word. Australia's new law bans prices the government “deems excessive,” and the quotation marks hint at the catch: someone in an office gets to decide what counts as excessive.

A profit margin is the slice of each sale a business actually keeps after paying its costs — sell a cup of lemonade for $1, spend 97 cents making it, and your margin is 3%. It's the article's key exhibit: supermarkets keep about 1 cent per dollar (Walmart, 4), while the big packaged-food makers keep about 13. Whoever's getting rich off your groceries, it isn't the store.

Wholesale prices are what stores pay when they buy goods in bulk from producers, before marking them up to the retail price you see on the shelf. The article's test: if grocers were profiteering, shelf prices would have raced ahead of wholesale prices — and they didn't.

Not focus — in economics, concentration measures how few companies control a market. A concentrated market (two or three giant chains, nowhere else to shop) hands those firms the power to overcharge. The article finds grocery markets mostly competitive, except in some rural counties where the nearest rival is a long drive away.

Market power is a company's ability to raise prices without losing its customers — usually because those customers have nowhere else to go. A monopoly has lots of it; a corner store in a crowded shopping district has none. Without market power, the gouging story falls apart.
As thin as a wafer — the crisp, papery cookie. A wafer-thin margin means the store keeps a sliver so slim (about 1 cent per dollar at Kroger) that there's simply no hidden fat in it to give back.

To milk customers is to squeeze money out of them steadily, the way you milk a cow — taking and taking as long as they'll stand there. Even Walmart's 4% margin “hardly looks like it is milking customers”: there just isn't much milk coming out.

Cream is the rich part that floats to the top of milk — so “the real cream” means the fattest profits. In the grocery world, the cream sits with the big food manufacturers (around 13% margins), not with the stores ringing you up (1–4%).

A supply chain is every link between a raw material and your hands: farmers grow it, manufacturers process it, distributors move it, stores sell it. The article's core move is walking up the chain link by link, checking where the money actually piles up — and it isn't at the checkout counter.

Not electrical sockets: an outlet is a store — a place where goods flow out to buyers. What matters for real competition is whether enough rival outlets sit within a distance shoppers could reasonably travel to buy groceries.

Inputs are everything that goes IN to producing something — fertiliser, fuel, seeds, workers' wages. The article's real culprit for pricey groceries: input costs surged (war in Ukraine, conflict with Iran, scarcer farm labor), and that push traveled all the way down the chain to your receipt.

Own-label brands — Americans say “store brands” — are products sold under the store's own name, like Walmart's Great Value, usually cheaper than the famous brands beside them. Shoppers defecting to own-label goods is what's been squeezing the big manufacturers' fat margins.

To slump is to sink or sag heavily — you slump in your chair; profits slump on a chart. The packaged-food giants have watched their margins slump for three years as shoppers trade down to cheaper store brands.

Subsidised means propped up with government money so something can charge less than its true cost (that's the British spelling — Americans write “subsidized”). Subsidised state stores could undercut everyone on price — which sounds great until the ordinary grocers competing with them go out of business.

An underserved area is one the market has neglected — too few stores, banks, or doctors for the people living there. The article concedes state stores “may have a useful role” in underserved rural spots where real competition never showed up.

A bread line is a queue of people waiting hours for basic food — the image history remembers from the state-run Soviet economy, where the shelves were often simply empty. The article's warning in a single picture: government supermarkets are remembered for their long bread lines, not their low bread prices.

The communist superpower (1922–1991) centered on Russia, where the government owned nearly everything — including almost every supermarket. Its chronic food shortages made it the standard cautionary tale about state-run shops.

State-run means owned and operated by the government — “the state” here is the government itself, not Texas or Ohio. Mamdani's proposed supermarkets would be government-run; the Soviet Union's almost all were.

To cook up an idea is to invent it, sometimes a bit hastily — like improvising a dish from whatever's in the fridge. The closing line — “politicians need to cook up some better ideas” — is a deliberate kitchen pun to end a story about food.

Developed countries are the rich, industrialized ones — America, Britain, Australia, France, Japan and their peers — as opposed to developing economies still building their wealth. The article keeps saying “in most developed countries” because that's the club its evidence covers.

Leftist means on the political left — favoring a bigger government role in the economy, more redistribution, and more public services. Canada's New Democratic Party is its major leftist party, and state grocery stores fit that worldview naturally.

Economists' standard yardstick for market concentration: square each company's share of the market and add them up — the higher the score, the closer the market is to a monopoly. Regulators lean on it when deciding whether to block mergers.
